idiom_name: generic type parameter constrained by a structural interface
implementation_notes: TypeScript keeps the 'policy as a type parameter' idea at the type level only: the host is generic over a policy type constrained structurally (class Cache<K, V, P extends EvictionPolicy<K>>), and because the constraint is erased at run time the policy call is still an ordinary property access - the parameter buys documentation and checking, not dispatch. The behaviour-bearing policy is normally a function or an object of functions injected into the host, and when the host should expose the policy's members itself the documented mixin pattern (class expressions typed with a constrained constructor, GConstructor<T>) is the closest analogue of policy inheritance. Use the type parameter when call sites should read as parameterized; use plain constructor injection when the policy is an implementation detail.
pitfalls: Type parameters are erased: two hosts with different policy type arguments are the same class at run time, so nothing stops a differently-shaped policy being passed through `as any`.
Structural constraints accept any accidental match (an object that happens to have `pick`); brand the policy interface with a unique member when accidental conformance matters.
Mixin composition copies prototype members and TypeScript cannot express higher-kinded policy application (a generic mixin over a generic base), so that route needs casts or concrete instantiations.
